summary.text: Using infinitude of the primes and the relation between prime counting and ordered prime indices, the proof first shows that \(a(n)\) is the least prime strictly greater than \(n^2\). Thus any prime between \(n^2\) and \((n+1)^2\) bounds \(a(n)\) from above, while conversely \(a(n)\) itself supplies such a prime whenever it lies below \((n+1)^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). Write
\[
\pi(x)=\#\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }p\le x\}
\]
for the usual prime-counting function. Let
\[
q_0<q_1<q_2<\cdots
\]
be the increasing enumeration of all primes, indexed starting at \(0\). Thus \(q_0=2,q_1=3,q_2=5\), and so forth. The sequence in the statement is defined by
\[
a(n)=q_{\pi(n^2)}.
\]
We will first justify carefully that this formula really gives the least prime strictly greater than \(n^2\).

The increasing enumeration \((q_j)_{j\ge0}\) exists for all indices because there are infinitely many primes. Indeed, primes are unbounded: given any \(B\in\mathbb N\), the integer
\[
N=(B+1)!+1
\]
is greater than \(1\), so it has a prime divisor \(r\). If \(r\le B\), then \(r\) divides \((B+1)!\), while by construction it also divides \((B+1)!+1\). It would therefore divide their difference \(1\), which is impossible for a prime. Hence \(r>B\). (The elementary fact that every integer greater than \(1\) has a prime divisor follows, for example, by taking its least divisor greater than \(1\): if that divisor were composite, one of its proper factors greater than \(1\) would be a smaller divisor.) Thus there is always another prime beyond any prescribed bound, and the primes can be listed increasingly as above.

It is useful to state the elementary counting-and-enumeration fact underlying the proof. For \(m\in\mathbb N\), put
\[
C(m)=\#\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p<m\}.
\]
Then
\[
q_{C(m)}=\min\{p:p\text{ is prime and }m\le p\}. \tag{1}
\]
To see this, let \(c=C(m)\). Since the \(q_j\)'s list all primes in strictly increasing order, the primes below \(m\) are precisely the initial segment
\[
q_0,q_1,\ldots,q_{c-1}
\]
(with the list empty if \(c=0\)). Consequently \(q_c\) is not below \(m\), so \(m\le q_c\). It is itself prime. If \(r\) is any prime with \(m\le r\), write \(r=q_j\), which is possible because the enumeration contains every prime. All \(c\) primes below \(m\) occur before \(r\), so \(c\le j\). Since the enumeration is increasing, \(q_c\le q_j=r\). Hence \(q_c\) is the least prime at least \(m\), proving (1). The set on the right of (1) is nonempty by the unboundedness of primes established above.

Now observe that
\[
\pi(n^2)=\#\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p\le n^2\}
       =\#\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p<n^2+1\}
       =C(n^2+1).
\]
Applying (1) with \(m=n^2+1\) gives
\[
a(n)=q_{\pi(n^2)}
    =\min\{p:p\text{ is prime and }n^2+1\le p\}.
\]
For natural numbers, \(n^2+1\le p\) is equivalent to \(n^2<p\). We have therefore proved the following three properties, valid in fact for every \(n\in\mathbb N\):

1. \(a(n)\) is prime;
2. \(n^2<a(n)\);
3. whenever \(p\) is prime and \(n^2<p\), one has \(a(n)\le p\).

In other words, \(a(n)\) is exactly the smallest prime strictly greater than \(n^2\).

We now prove the desired equivalence.

First assume Legendre's conjecture in the form appearing in the statement: for every positive integer \(n\), there is a prime \(p\) such that
\[
n^2<p<(n+1)^2.
\]
Fix any \(n>0\). Choose such a prime \(p\). Since \(a(n)\) is the least prime strictly greater than \(n^2\), property 3 gives
\[
a(n)\le p.
\]
Combining this with \(p<(n+1)^2\) yields
\[
a(n)<(n+1)^2.
\]
Because \(n>0\) was arbitrary, this proves
\[
\forall n\in\mathbb N,\quad n>0\Longrightarrow a(n)<(n+1)^2.
\]

Conversely, assume that for every positive integer \(n\),
\[
a(n)<(n+1)^2.
\]
Fix \(n>0\), and take
\[
p=a(n).
\]
By properties 1 and 2 above, \(p\) is prime and
\[
n^2<p.
\]
The present assumption supplies the other strict inequality
\[
p=a(n)<(n+1)^2.
\]
Thus
\[
n^2<p<(n+1)^2
\]
for a prime \(p\). Since this construction works for every \(n>0\), Legendre's conjecture in the stated form follows.

Therefore
\[
\left(\forall n>0,\ \exists p\text{ prime with }n^2<p<(n+1)^2\right)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left(\forall n>0,\ a(n)<(n+1)^2\right),
\]
as required.
